job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Daria Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I finished a business administration degree with an accounting focus at Stannard University in June, and I'm back home in Pellham, living in the flat above my family's hardware shop, Quinn and Daughters. I get up at six, open the shop with my dad, do the till and the stock book until nine, then send applications from the back office. Wednesdays I sing in the church choir and Sundays I go to lunch at my gran's.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of all that, and what part do you still like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hardest part is that I'm doing everything right and it isn't working. I've written to about thirty local firms and had one proper interview. What I still love is the books: at my internship with Harlan and Dyce, a three-person accounting practice on Church Street, I kept the ledgers for the farm clients, and I liked that every number had a person and a field behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I hoped. Hype passes and good, honest work stays. I'd tell my friends at church that the old ways of doing business, with a handshake and a proper ledger, still count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm no better off. I have a degree, some student debt and about two months of savings, and I still don't have a real job. My worry isn't AI, it's that small local firms like Harlan and Dyce don't take on new people, and I'm too picky to move to the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending letters and visiting firms in person, because a letter on paper gets read in a town like this. I'd keep working at the shop for my dad and take on the books for two or three small neighbours. I wouldn't touch AI tools, because I don't see the need and I don't trust them with accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels tiring and a bit shaming. I don't like asking my parents to carry me, and I feel it every time I take wages from the till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you are doing everything right. What would you do if the search stayed stuck for another year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it went on a year, I'd ask Mr Harlan to take me on part-time for little money so I could learn the practice. And I'd keep the shop, since it's solid. Some of us just need a family business to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your father say about the situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad says, 'Work is work, take what's in front of you.' He doesn't say it unkindly, but I hear what he means, which is that I should think about the shop more seriously.

say: I'd tell friends at church that **old ways of business** still count, like a handshake and a ledger.
I'd say hype passes and **honest work stays**.
think: My worry isn't AI, it's that **small local firms** don't take on new people.
I'm **too picky** to move to the city, and I know it.
do: Send **paper letters** and visit local firms in person.
Keep working at **my dad's shop** and take on the books for two or three neighbours.
Stay away from **AI tools**, because I don't trust them with accounts.
feel: It feels **tiring and shaming**, especially taking wages from the till.
S0.quote: I don't like asking my parents to carry me, and I feel it every time I take wages from the till.
fieldNote: Daria's strain is **personal and moral**: pride, family help and no real job.
She prefers **in-person, paper and local** routes, which matches her resistant style.
The family shop is both **her safety net and** her guilt.

steps.text: Visit local accounting firms in person with a paper letter
Keep the Quinn and Daughters stock book and till
Do the books for three small neighbours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful about racing ahead. I'd say a firm that dumps its people for software has forgotten what a business is for, and I'd say that out loud at church and at the shop counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the ledgers and the sums are the first to go. Checking figures and filling in returns are what a junior does, so Harlan and Dyce will need one person where they might have needed two. I could be the one who doesn't get hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a local apprenticeship if one is offered, even if it pays little, because that's how my grandfather learned. I'd keep the shop work going, and I'd try the one thing my dad suggests, which is getting the shop's stock on a simple program. I'd do that with him beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels unsettling, like the town changing around me. I'd feel slightly angry at the people selling this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the tasks at Harlan and Dyce would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The data entry and the checking go first. What stays is knowing the farmer, going to the farm, and a signature from somebody who answers for it. That's what a small firm sells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want an employer to do for graduates like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to take on young people for a fixed apprenticeship, with a proper wage, and train us properly. I don't want a handout. I want the chance to learn the trade from someone who has done it.

say: I'd say a firm that **dumps its people** for software has forgotten what a business is for.
I'd say it **at church** and at the shop counter.
think: The ledgers and sums go first, so Harlan and Dyce will want **one person instead of** two.
I could be the one **who doesn't get hired**.
do: Take a **local apprenticeship** even if it pays little, as my grandfather did.
Keep the **shop work** going and help my dad put stock on a simple program.
Try that **program only with him** beside me.
feel: It feels **unsettling**, like the town changing around me.
S1.quote: I don't want a handout. I want the chance to learn the trade from someone who has done it.
fieldNote: Daria's answer is **moral and local**: she blames firms that drop people, not the tools.
She asks for **apprenticeships**, in line with her traditional view, not handouts.
She would only try new tools **with her dad beside** her.

steps.text: Take a local apprenticeship at a small firm
Keep the shop till and stock work going
Set up stock tracking at the shop with my dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that this is not something a town can handle alone, and I'd say it shouldn't be left to the big companies. I'd want families and churches to be ready, and I'd want leaders to say what they're doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be frightened, to be honest. If all thinking work is gone in two years, my degree isn't worth the paper, and a three-person practice can't hire me. I don't know what I'm for, and I have no second plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the shop and learn everything about it, the stock, the suppliers, the customers, so I'm useful there whatever happens. I'd cut all spending and tell my parents everything the first week. I'd also ask the pastor whether the church has a fund or a list of people who need help. I'd put the savings in the bank and not touch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like losing the floor under my feet. I'd cry first and then I'd work, and I'd probably not sleep for the first month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what happens to the plan to wait for a local firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plan to wait for a local firm is over. A firm that's three people wouldn't survive when the software does everything. I'd be the daughter in the shop instead, and I don't mind that, but I feel I've wasted three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, 'I'm going to be here a long time, and I'll work for my keep.' My mum would cry and my dad would say 'Good,' and then we'd sit at the kitchen table and write down what the shop can afford.

say: I'd say this is **not something a town** can handle alone or leave to big companies.
I'd want **leaders to say** what they are doing.
think: If all thinking work is gone in two years, my degree is **not worth the paper**.
I don't know **what I'm for**, and I have no second plan.
do: Stay at the **shop** and learn its stock, suppliers and customers.
Tell my **parents everything** in the first week and cut all spending.
Ask the **pastor** whether the church has a fund for people who need help.
feel: It feels like **losing the floor** under my feet.
S2.quote: I don't know what I'm for, and I have no second plan.
fieldNote: Daria has **no plan B** and says so, which is why panicked is honest here.
Her fallback is **family and church**, in line with her traditional outlook.
She says she doesn't mind the shop but feels **three years were wasted**.

steps.text: Learn every part of the shop's stock and suppliers
Ask the pastor about church support
Put all savings in the bank and not touch them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a town to get ready if it starts now. I'd say we should be teaching apprenticeships again, and I'd say it to anyone who'll listen after the Sunday service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be afraid, but I could breathe. I could get an apprenticeship or a job at the shop, work for four years, and be useful to somebody when it comes. The shop is hands-on, so it's got an extra three years of safety before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in the shop full-time, take on the books for a few neighbours, and try again for a local apprenticeship in the spring. I'd start learning how to do orders on the computer with my dad. I'd save every spare pound, and I'd ask my parents to teach me how the shop makes its money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long cold winter that you can see coming. I don't panic with five years, but my stomach tightens when I read about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for the family shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop can keep going because people always want screws, paint and someone to ask. I'd want to learn to run it, not just serve in it, so that when my dad retires there's someone who knows the books and the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you like the town to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the town to bring back apprenticeships and to help the small firms keep taking people on. A town that stops training its own young people has forgotten how to survive.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to get ready** if the town starts now.
I'd say we should **bring back apprenticeships**.
think: I'd still be afraid, but I could **breathe**.
The shop is hands-on, so it has **three extra years** before robots.
do: Work in the **shop full-time** and keep the neighbours' books.
Apply again for a **local apprenticeship** in the spring.
Learn **computer ordering** with my dad and ask my parents how the shop makes money.
feel: It feels like a **long cold winter** you can see coming.
S3.quote: A town that stops training its own young people has forgotten how to survive.
fieldNote: More time lets Daria **breathe**, but she is still jobless today, so alarmed.
She sees the **hands-on shop** as a three-year shelter.
Her call for **apprenticeships** returns here, tied to her view of community.

steps.text: Work full-time at the family shop
Apply again for a local apprenticeship in spring
Learn the shop's online ordering with my dad
Ask my parents how the shop makes its money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it properly. I'd say the churches, the schools and the small firms should work together to get young people trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be much calmer. In ten years I could get a job, pay my debt, perhaps marry and take on the shop. I'd still be a bit nervous in the last years, but my parents would be settled and I'd have a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job I can get and do it well, then work my way up in a small firm or in the shop. I'd learn a bit of the computer side as it becomes normal, a bit at a time. I'd save for a house and keep going to choir, because I want a settled life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable. It's like a long road, and a long road is easier for someone who prefers to walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what does your life look like if things go well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it goes well, I'm 33, married, with a child, and I run Quinn and Daughters with a good accountant's eye. My parents would be retired and proud, and the shop would still be on Main Street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you even with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would worry me is that I wouldn't use the time well. I could just keep waiting like I am now, and ten years would go by, and I'd be left behind.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** to do it properly.
I'd say **churches, schools and small** firms should train young people together.
think: In ten years I could **get a job**, pay my debt and take on the shop.
I'd be a bit nervous in the **last years**.
do: Take **any job** and do it well, then work up in a small firm or the shop.
Learn the **computer side** gradually, as it becomes normal.
**Save for a house** and keep going to choir.
feel: It feels **manageable**, like a long road for someone who prefers to walk.
S4.quote: If it goes well, I'm 33, married, with a child, and I run Quinn and Daughters with a good accountant's eye.
fieldNote: Daria's goals are **family and community**: marriage, a child, the shop and choir.
Her unease eases with a decade but the **jobless present** keeps it at anxious.
She names her own risk: **waiting too long** and losing the time.

steps.text: Take any local job and do it well
Learn the shop's computer systems gradually
Plan marriage and a family within ten years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no plan and no time to make one. What would help is local apprenticeships that pay a proper wage and leaders who say plainly what they will do for families.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that not everyone my age wants to start a company or move to the city. Some of us want to work in the town we grew up in, and I'd like the people planning the future to remember us.

headlineQuote: Not everyone my age wants to start a company or move to the city.
portrait: Daria is a 23-year-old **business graduate** living above the family hardware shop in Pellham, with no offer.
She has some debt, two months of savings and **never uses AI tools**.
She is traditional, church-going and wants **apprenticeships** and family support, not handouts.
Her mood climbs from anxious to **panicked at two years**, because she has no second plan and prefers the familiar.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, as she'd have no plan and no time to make one.
whatWouldHelp: **Properly paid local apprenticeships** and leaders who plainly say what they'll do for families would help.
